arXiv:2303.16607v2 [math.PR] 01 May 2024

Spectral gap of the symmetric inclusion process

Seonwoo Kim and Federico Sau Address: Seonwoo Kim
Department of Mathematical Sciences, Seoul National University, Seoul, Republic of Korea Email address: ksw6leta@snu.ac.kr Address: Federico Sau
Dipartimento di Matematica, Informatica e Geoscienze, Università degli Studi di Trieste, Trieste, Italy Email address: federico.sau@units.it
Abstract.

We consider the symmetric inclusion process on a general finite graph. Our main result establishes universal upper and lower bounds for the spectral gap of this interacting particle system in terms of the spectral gap of the random walk on the same graph. In the regime in which the gamma-like reversible measures of the particle systems are log-concave, our bounds match, yielding a version for the symmetric inclusion process of the celebrated Aldous’ spectral gap conjecture originally formulated for the interchange process. Finally, by means of duality techniques, we draw analogous conclusions for an interacting diffusion-like unbounded conservative spin system known as Brownian energy process.

Key words and phrases:
Interacting particle systems; unbounded conservative spin systems; spectral gap; symmetric inclusion process; Brownian energy process
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 60K35; secondary 60J27, 05C50.

1. Introduction, models, and main results

Establishing spectral gap inequalities is a central topic in the analysis of convergence to equilibrium for large scale stochastic dynamics. In the context of interacting particle systems (e.g., [Lig05]), a spectral gap estimate with a sharp dependence on the system size grants a good control on the local mixing properties of the dynamics. This yields a number of applications, for instance, in scaling limits and metastability (e.g., [KL99, GJ14, LMS23] and references therein).

In this paper, we focus on spectral gap inequalities for a specific model, namely the symmetric inclusion process (SIP). This process was first introduced in [GKR07] as a particle analogue of statistical mechanics’ models of interacting diffusions, and corresponds to a spatial version of the mean-field Moran model with mutation from population genetics (e.g., [Cor23]). SIP is also related to SEP, i.e., the symmetric exclusion process (e.g., [CLR10]): SEP’s hard-core exclusion interaction is replaced here by attraction between particles.

SIP has been shown to exhibit interesting qualitative behaviors, such as condensation and metastability in the limit of vanishing diffusivity α→0\alpha\to 0 (e.g., [GRV11, GRV13, BDG17, JCG20, Kim21, KS21], see also Section 1.3.5 below), representations in terms of Lie algebras and limit theorems out of equilibrium have also been rigorously investigated (e.g., [GKRV09, FGS22, DSPS24]). The present work represents a first step in the quantitative analysis of convergence to equilibrium for this interacting particle system, together with the same analysis for a related diffusion-like unbounded spin system called the Brownian energy process.

1.1. SIP and its spectral gap

Let G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}) be a connected weighted finite graph, with |V|=n|V|=n sites and symmetric non-negative edge-weights, i.e., cx​y=cy​x≥0c_{xy}=c_{yx}\geq 0 for all x,y∈Vx,y\in V. For any positive site-weights α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V} and k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} total number of particles, we let SIPk​(G,α){\rm SIP}_{k}(G,\alpha) be defined as the Markov process (η⁡(t))t≥0(\eta(t))_{t\geq 0} on the configuration space with kk particles

Ξk:={η∈ℕ0V:|η|=k},|η|:=∑x∈Vηx,\Xi_{k}:=\left\{\eta\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{V}:|\eta|=k\right\}\ ,\qquad|\eta|:=\sum_{x\in V}\eta_{x}\ ,

and with infinitesimal generator LkL_{k} given, for all functions f∈ℝΞkf\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}}, by

(1.1) Lk​f​(η)=∑x∈Vηx​∑y∈Vcx​y​(αy+ηy)​(f⁡(η−δx+δy)−f⁡(η)),η∈Ξk.L_{k}f(\eta)=\sum_{x\in V}\eta_{x}\sum_{y\in V}c_{xy}\,(\alpha_{y}+\eta_{y})\left(f(\eta-\delta_{x}+\delta_{y})-f(\eta)\right)\ ,\qquad\eta\in\Xi_{k}\ .

In this formula, η−δx+δy\eta-\delta_{x}+\delta_{y} denotes the configuration in Ξk\Xi_{k} obtained from η\eta (with ηx≥1\eta_{x}\geq 1) by moving a particle from site xx to yy. We observe that, if (αy+ηy)\left(\alpha_{y}+\eta_{y}\right) were to be replaced by (1−ηy)\left(1-\eta_{y}\right), LkL_{k} in (1.1) would describe a SEP-dynamics (e.g., [CLR10]); while, if cx​y≡1/nc_{xy}\equiv 1/n, we would obtain the Moran model with parent-independent mutation (e.g., [Cor23]).

For each k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, due to the connectedness of the graph GG, the generator LkL_{k} describes an irreducible Markov chain with a unique invariant measure, which we call μα,k\mu_{\alpha,k}. As a simple detailed balance computation shows, the particle system is actually reversible with respect to μα,k\mu_{\alpha,k}, which reads as follows:

(1.2) μα,k​(η)=1Zα,k​∏x∈VΓ⁡(αx+ηx)Γ⁡(αx)​ηx!,η∈Ξk,\mu_{\alpha,k}(\eta)=\frac{1}{Z_{\alpha,k}}\prod_{x\in V}\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_{x}+\eta_{x})}{\Gamma(\alpha_{x})\,\eta_{x}!}\ ,\qquad\eta\in\Xi_{k}\ ,

with

Zα,k:=Γ⁡(|α|+k)Γ⁡(|α|)​k!,|α|:=∑x∈Vαx,Z_{\alpha,k}:=\frac{\Gamma(|\alpha|+k)}{\Gamma(|\alpha|)\,k!}\ ,\qquad|\alpha|:=\sum_{x\in V}\alpha_{x}\ ,

being the normalization constant. Here, Γ⁡(β)\Gamma(\beta) is the usual gamma function, for which we recall Γ(β+ℓ)/Γ(β)=β(β+1)⋯(β+ℓ−1)\Gamma(\beta+\ell)/\Gamma(\beta)=\beta\left(\beta+1\right)\cdots\left(\beta+\ell-1\right) for β>0\beta>0 and ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in\mathbb{N}.

By the ergodic theorem for finite-state Markov chains, the law of the kk-particle system converges in the long-run to the invariant measure μα,k\mu_{\alpha,k}. Moreover, since the process is reversible, the generator LkL_{k} has real and non-positive eigenvalues

−λk,|Ξk|−1≤…≤−λk,1<−λk,0=0,-\lambda_{k,|\Xi_{k}|-1}\leq\ldots\leq-\lambda_{k,1}<-\lambda_{k,0}=0\ ,

and all admit a variational characterization. Among these, the spectral gap — namely, the second smallest eigenvalue of −Lk-L_{k} — measures the exponential rate of such a convergence, e.g., for all times t≥0t\geq 0,

exp(−λk,1t)≤supη∈Ξk2‖μtη−μα,k‖TV≤(minη∈Ξkμα,k(η))−1/2exp(−λk,1t),\exp(-\lambda_{k,1}t)\leq\sup_{\eta\in\Xi_{k}}2\left\|\mu^{\eta}_{t}-\mu_{\alpha,k}\right\|_{\rm TV}\leq\left(\min_{\eta\in\Xi_{k}}\mu_{\alpha,k}(\eta)\right)^{-1/2}\exp(-\lambda_{k,1}t)\ ,

where ‖⋅‖TV\left\|\,\cdot\,\right\|_{\rm TV} denotes the total-variation norm, while OPENμtη=Law⁡(η⁡(t)))\mu^{\eta}_{t}={\rm Law}(\eta(t))) when η⁡(0)=η∈Ξk\eta(0)=\eta\in\Xi_{k}. We refer the interested reader to, e.g., [SC97] for more details on these classical bounds.

In what follows, we let

gapk(G,α):=λk,1\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{k}(G,\alpha):=\lambda_{k,1}

denote the spectral gap of SIPk​(G,α){\rm SIP}_{k}(G,\alpha). Our main goal is to estimate gapk(G,α)\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{k}(G,\alpha) in terms of the spectral gap of the corresponding random walk on the same graph, i.e., the Markov process, referred to as RW⁡(G,α){\rm RW}(G,\alpha), on VV with generator AαA_{\alpha} acting on functions f∈ℝVf\in\mathbb{R}^{V} as

Aα​f​(x)=∑y∈Vcx​y​αy​(f⁡(y)−f⁡(x)),x∈V.A_{\alpha}f(x)=\sum_{y\in V}c_{xy}\,\alpha_{y}\left(f(y)-f(x)\right)\ ,\qquad x\in V\ .

Since the rate to jump from site xx to yy equals cx​y​αyc_{xy}\,\alpha_{y}, detailed balance shows that the reversible measure for RW⁡(G,α){\rm RW}(G,\alpha) is proportional to α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V}.

We observe that SIPk​(G,α){\rm SIP}_{k}(G,\alpha) with just one particle (k=1k=1) corresponds to a single random walk (thus, non-interacting) evolving like RW⁡(G,α){\rm RW}(G,\alpha) on the sites of GG; the non-trivial inclusion interaction between particles occurs as soon as k≥2k\geq 2. Let

gapSIP(G,α):=infk≥2gapk(G,α)andgapRW(G,α):=gap1(G,α)\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha):=\inf_{k\geq 2}\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{k}(G,\alpha)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha):=\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{1}(G,\alpha)

denote the spectral gaps of the interacting particle system and of the random walk, respectively. We are now ready to state our main result.

Theorem 1.1.

For every G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}) and α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V},

(1∧αmin)​gapRW(G,α)≤gapSIP(G,α)≤gapRW(G,α),\left(1\wedge\alpha_{\rm min}\right)\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha)\leq\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha)\leq\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha)\ ,

where αmin:=minx∈V⁡αx\alpha_{\rm min}:=\min_{x\in V}\alpha_{x}.

These bounds can be used to efficiently estimate the spectral gap of SIP{\rm SIP} in concrete examples. Remarkably, we observe that the inequalities in Theorem 1.1 saturate to identities as soon as αmin≥1\alpha_{\rm min}\geq 1 (which is equivalent to the log-concavity of μα,k\mu_{\alpha,k}), yielding the following spectral gaps’ identity:

Corollary 1.2.

For every G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}) and α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V} such that αmin≥1\alpha_{\rm min}\geq 1,

(1.3) gapSIP(G,α)=gapRW(G,α).\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha)=\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha)\ .

The result in Corollary 1.2 may be interpreted as a SIP{\rm SIP}’s version of the celebrated Aldous’ spectral gap conjecture, originally formulated for the interchange process and SEP{\rm SEP}, and recently solved by Caputo et al. in [CLR10]. An identity of the type (1.3) may be viewed as an exact tensorization of the Poincaré inequality over the kk components, a property which trivially holds when considering kk independent particles. Such an identity is, in general, not expected to hold for truly interacting systems. This property — apart from situations in which the spectrum is fully explicit (e.g., [Shi77, Gri14, Cor23]) — has been established on any graph only for a few examples other than the interchange process and SEP:

  • •

    SEP{\rm SEP} in contact with reservoirs in [Sal23, Sal24];

  • •

    the binomial splitting process in [QS23] (see also [BC24]).

Corollary 1.2 proves that SIP{\rm SIP} with αmin≥1\alpha_{\rm min}\geq 1 also satisfies this exact tensorization property. See also Section 1.3.2 for a more detailed discussion on Aldous’ spectral gap conjecture and related work.

1.2. BEP and its spectral gap

The Brownian energy process (BEP) is an interacting system of continuous spins placed on the sites of a graph (e.g., [GKRV09]). This process falls into the larger class of unbounded conservative spin systems, and is intimately related to SIP{\rm SIP}. The spins (or, energies) evolve as diffusions. Moreover, the dynamics preserves the total amount of energy of the system, and is reversible with respect to measures associated to gamma distributions. Just like SIP and the Moran model are related, the BEP{\rm BEP} on the complete graph corresponds to the multi-type Wright-Fisher diffusion with mutation.

Let us now describe the model more formally. Given a graph GG and site-weights α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V}, the BEP⁡(G,α){\rm BEP}(G,\alpha) is the diffusion process (ζ⁡(t))t≥0(\zeta(t))_{t\geq 0} on [0,∞)V[0,\infty)^{V}, whose infinitesimal evolution is described by the following generator:

(1.4) ℒ=12∑x,y∈Vcx​y{−(αyζx−αxζy)(∂ζx−∂ζy)+ζxζy(∂ζx−∂ζy)2}.\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x,y\in V}c_{xy}\left\{-\left(\alpha_{y}\,\zeta_{x}-\alpha_{x}\,\zeta_{y}\right)\left(\partial_{\zeta_{x}}-\partial_{\zeta_{y}}\right)+\zeta_{x}\,\zeta_{y}\left(\partial_{\zeta_{x}}-\partial_{\zeta_{y}}\right)^{2}\right\}\ .

The diffusion (ζ⁡(t))t≥0(\zeta(t))_{t\geq 0} admits νθ:=⊗x∈VGamma(αx,θ)\nu_{\theta}:=\otimes_{x\in V}\,{\rm Gamma}(\alpha_{x},\theta), θ>0\theta>0, as a one-parameter family of reversible product measures, fully supported on [0,∞)V[0,\infty)^{V}. However, all features of the system are well-captured by the dynamics which only considers configurations with unit total energy: on the one side, applying the generator ℒ\mathcal{L} to the function ζ↦|ζ|:=∑x∈Vζx\zeta\mapsto|\zeta|:=\sum_{x\in V}\zeta_{x} shows that the dynamics conserves the total energy of the system; on the other side, a simple scaling argument demonstrates that the action of ℒ\mathcal{L} does not depend on |ζ||\zeta|. Therefore, all throughout, it suffices to consider ζ⁡(t)\zeta(t) as evolving on ΔV\Delta_{V}, the simplex of probability measures on VV, for which π:=νθ(⋅∣ζ∈ΔV)\pi:=\nu_{\theta}(\,\cdot\mid\zeta\in\Delta_{V}), θ>0\theta>0, is reversible, and given by

π⁡(d​ζ)=(1B⁡(α)​∏x∈Vζxαx−1)​d​ζ,with​ζ∈ΔV,B⁡(α):=∏x∈VΓ⁡(αx)Γ⁡(|α|),\pi({\rm d}\zeta)=\left(\frac{1}{B(\alpha)}\prod_{x\in V}\zeta_{x}^{\alpha_{x}-1}\right){\rm d}\zeta\ ,\qquad\text{with}\ \zeta\in\Delta_{V}\ ,\ B(\alpha):=\frac{\prod_{x\in V}\Gamma(\alpha_{x})}{\Gamma(|\alpha|)}\ ,

where d​ζ{\rm d}\zeta denotes the uniform measure on ΔV\Delta_{V}. Note that π\pi is independent of θ>0\theta>0.

Quantifying the exponential rate of convergence to equilibrium goes through a spectral analysis of the generator ℒ\mathcal{L} on L2​(ΔV,π)L^{2}(\Delta_{V},\pi). Since ℒ\mathcal{L} is self-adjoint on L2​(ΔV,π)L^{2}(\Delta_{V},\pi), its spectrum is real. Moreover, as we will show in Section 4, −ℒ-\mathcal{L} is non-negative and has a pure-point spectrum, with only one zero eigenvalue corresponding to the constant eigenfunction.

In our next result, we provide an analogue of Theorem 1.1 for gapBEP​(G,α)>0{\rm gap}_{\rm BEP}(G,\alpha)>0, the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of −ℒ-\mathcal{L} on L2​(ΔV,π)L^{2}(\Delta_{V},\pi).

Theorem 1.3.

For every G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}) and α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V},

(1∧αmin)​gapRW(G,α)≤gapBEP(G,α)≤gapRW(G,α).\left(1\wedge\alpha_{\rm min}\right)\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha)\leq\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm BEP}(G,\alpha)\leq\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha)\ .

Hence, provided αmin≥1\alpha_{\rm min}\geq 1,

(1.5) gapBEP(G,α)=gapRW(G,α).\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm BEP}(G,\alpha)=\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha)\ .

1.3. Related work, proof strategy, and open problems

1.3.1. Functional inequalities and comparison techniques

Functional inequalities play a major role in PDE and probability theory, and several approaches have been developed for this purpose. Comparison techniques (e.g., [SC97, MT06]) are among the most robust and well-established ones, and proved to be especially effective when estimating spectral gaps (or Poincaré constants, their inverses), log-Sobolev constants, and Nash inequalities.

In the more specific context of interacting particle systems and unbounded spin systems subjected to conservation laws, comparing Dirichlet forms is key in the so-called martingale method and its variants (e.g., [Qua92, LY93, DSC93, LSV96, JLQY99, LPY02, Cap03, Cap04, Cap08, Sas13] and references therein). In a nutshell, this strategy compares the system’s Dirichlet form on the geometry of interest (e.g., SEP on ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d}-boxes of size ℓ\ell), to that on more tractable geometries (e.g., the complete graph), and finally transfers the gained information back through a path counting argument. In most examples, this method captures the correct dependence on the size ℓ\ell of the system, but the universal prefactor is typically not optimal (e.g., it deteriorates with dd, the dimension of the box).

1.3.2. Aldous’ spectral gap conjecture and related examples

Sharper identities like the one expressed in Aldous’ spectral gap conjecture [CLR10] holding true on general graphs have been verified only for a handful of models (as already discussed below Corollary 1.2), each of these examples requiring ad hoc proof arguments.

The proof in [CLR10] for the interchange process and SEP combines in a non-trivial way a nonlinear network reduction and a hard correlation inequality (which became known as Octopus inequality). The first ingredient allows an induction argument on nn, the size of the graph, well-compatible with the particle-hole symmetry of SEP. Such a symmetry (or, alternatively, the fact that SEP may be obtained as a projection of the interchange process) is a property that seems to be lacking for SIP.

Negative dependence — a form of negativity of correlations of all orders — is nicely exploited in [Sal23] for the non-conservative reversible SEP. We remark that SIP is positive (rather than negative) dependent, see, e.g., [GRV10, FRS22].

The arguments in [QS23] for the binomial splitting process build on a L2L^{2}-contraction inequality established in [AL12] for the “dual” averaging process. the BEP{\rm BEP} is one of the continuum duals of SIP (e.g., [GKRV09]); nevertheless, the analogue of such a contraction estimate is not known for the BEP{\rm BEP}.

1.3.3. Discussion on proof strategy

Our approach combines in an elementary way two main ingredients:

  • •

    self-duality of the interacting particle system;

  • •

    comparison inequalities.

Self-duality/consistency of SIP (cf. (2.3) and (3.3) below) ensures a certain rigidity and structure of eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. This immediately yields the upper bound in Theorem 1.1 (Section 2), and this is what allows to effectively set off an induction argument on kk, the total number of particles (rather than nn, the size of the graph, as in [CLR10]), for the lower bound in Section 3. We mention that an analogous consistency-based characterization of eigenspaces found application also in the proof of [QS23, Theorem 2.1] on the spectral gap of the binomial splitting process.

In closing the proof of the induction step from k−1k-1 to kk, we employ comparison inequalities. Inspired by the recent work [HS19] on zero-range dynamics, in Lemma 3.3 we rearrange SIP’s Dirichlet form so to reduce our task to an estimate of the spectral gap not of the whole system, but rather of the kkth particle only, uniformly over the positions of the remaining k−1k-1 particles. Finally, the min-max theorem for eigenvalues (e.g., [SC97, Theorem 1.2.10]) yields the desired single-particle spectral gap inequality (Lemma 3.4). For this step, we compare both Dirichlet forms and L2L^{2}-norms of such a particle to those of a non-interacting walk. We emphasize that, although the estimate that we get in Lemma 3.4 deteriorates by a factor kk, the reduction applied in Lemma 3.3 returns back exactly the same factor kk, thus, allows us to conclude the proof for SIP’s spectral gap estimates.

The analogous result for the BEP{\rm BEP} is derived by remapping SIP into the BEP{\rm BEP} via an intertwining relation, translating all spectral information from the particle to the diffusion system.

1.3.4. Spectral gap identity and Gibbs samplers

Focusing on interacting systems on more specific graphs, a spectral gap identity in the spirit of that in (1.3) has been proved on 1D geometries also for two models of continuous spins with Gibbs sampler dynamics in [CLL20, CLL22]. Especially the first one of these models studied in [CLL20] is relevant for the present work. Indeed, when considered on a general graph G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}) and with general site-weights α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V}, the model studied in [CLL20] corresponds to the Gibbs sampler of BEP⁡(G,α){\rm BEP}(G,\alpha): instead of letting energies diffuse as in the BEP{\rm BEP}, the energies are instantaneously set to their local beta-like equilibrium among randomly chosen edges.

While our Theorem 1.3 shows that, as soon as αmin≥1\alpha_{\rm min}\geq 1, (1.5) for the BEP{\rm BEP} holds on any graph, rather surprisingly an analogous identity for its Gibbs sampler version fails on specific geometries. Indeed, the proof in [CLL20] crucially relies on the one-dimensional structure of the model, which grants a monotonicity property of the spectral gap’s eigenfunction (similar to that for birth-and-death chains). However, as discussed in [CLL20, Remark 4], the mean-field version of the same model provides a counterexample to such an identity.

The aforementioned Gibbs sampler version of the BEP{\rm BEP} may also be regarded as arising from a procedure of “instantaneous thermalization” among edges. Instantaneous thermalizations of this kind have been studied for several particle and energy models (e.g., [GKRV09, Section 6.3]), and it is well-known that, at least for symmetric systems, this procedure does not alter qualitative properties of the system as, e.g., the form of the reversible measures and the richness of the duality relations. Nonetheless, it does affect dramatically the eigenstructure of the processes and other quantitative features determining convergence to equilibrium, as the comparison between the model in [CLL20] and our result on the BEP illustrates. We emphasize that this example also shows that (self-)duality does not guarantee per se the validity of a spectral gap identity.

1.3.5. Open problems

Besides the problem of quantifying the sensitivity with respect to Gibbs-sampler perturbations of the model (as discussed in, e.g., [CLL20, Section 1.2]; see also the previous paragraph), settling the role of the threshold αmin=1\alpha_{\rm min}=1 remains open. More specifically, our results provide only partial answers in the regime

αmin∈(0,1).\alpha_{\rm min}\in(0,1)\ .

This regime corresponds, roughly speaking, to the case in which particle/energy interaction becomes predominant over the mechanism of independent diffusion. Here, our results state that a spectral gap comparison is robust over the underlying geometry G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}), but do not say anything about the sharpness of the first-order dependence on the parameter αmin∈(0,1)\alpha_{\rm min}\in(0,1). We emphasize that such a threshold appears also in other related works, e.g., [CLL20, pp. 2453–4], as well as [BW09, LP22], and also there sharp results are not available.

When αmin∈(0,1)\alpha_{\rm min}\in(0,1), we observe that our proof techniques fail to give matching upper and lower bounds for gapSIP\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm SIP} as in (1.3). On the one hand, elementary examples with small graphs show that our bounds cannot be generally improved. For instance, consider the segment {1,2,3,4}\{1,2,3,4\} with n=4n=4 sites; in this context, it is not difficult to check that the lower bound in Lemma 3.4 is essentially sharp (take there, e.g., ξ=ℓ​δ1+(k−ℓ−1)​δ4∈Ξk−1\xi=\ell\delta_{1}+(k-\ell-1)\delta_{4}\in\Xi_{k-1}, with ℓ≈k/2\ell\approx k/2). On the other hand, on the complete graph (cx​y≡1/nc_{xy}\equiv 1/n) the spectrum of −Lk-L_{k} is fully explicit and given (without counting multiplicities) by (e.g., [Shi77, Cor23])

ℓn​(|α|+ℓ−1),ℓ=0,1,…,k.\frac{\ell}{n}\left(|\alpha|+\ell-1\right)\ ,\qquad\ell=0,1,\ldots,k\ .

Hence, the spectral gap identity in (1.3) holds true for all positive site-weights α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V} in this mean-field setting, without any restriction on αmin>0\alpha_{\rm min}>0. These considerations somehow suggest that, in the regime αmin∈(0,1)\alpha_{\rm min}\in(0,1), mean-field features (irrelevant when αmin≥1\alpha_{\rm min}\geq 1) of the underlying geometry could be decisive for the validity of a spectral gap identity.

Since spectral gap identities are not available when αmin∈(0,1)\alpha_{\rm min}\in(0,1), yet, a sensible open question concerns the limiting behavior of gapSIP​(G,α){\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha) when taking αmin≪1\alpha_{\rm min}\ll 1. As studied in [GRV13, BDG17], a non-trivial metastable picture of SIPk​(G,α){\rm SIP}_{k}(G,\alpha) emerges in this asymptotic regime αx≡α→0\alpha_{x}\equiv\alpha\to 0 on the timescale α−1\alpha^{-1}, provided that k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, the total number of particles, is not too large compared to α−1≫1\alpha^{-1}\gg 1 (namely, log⁡k≪α−1\log k\ll\alpha^{-1}). In addition to this, α−1\alpha^{-1} was also proved to be the slowest (and actually the unique) relevant timescale for this metastable system, in the sense that macroscopic order statistics of the system reached stationarity not later than times t≈α−1t\approx\alpha^{-1}. Given the well-known interpretation of spectral gap as governing the rate to relaxation-to-equilibrium of reversible Markov processes (e.g., [SC97]), and since gapRW(α)≈α−1\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm RW}(\alpha)\approx\alpha^{-1} as α→0\alpha\to 0, this suggests — at least at the heuristic level — that gapSIP(α)≈gapRW(α)\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm SIP}(\alpha)\approx\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm RW}(\alpha). If this were true, the lower bound in Theorem 1.1 would not capture this because of the extra factor αmin≪1\alpha_{\rm min}\ll 1.

We conclude that we expect some comparisons and decompositions, which we developed for the analysis of gapSIP​(G,α){\rm gap}_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha), to turn useful also for other particle systems with gamma-like reversible measures. Examples of such models include the beta binomial splitting process (e.g., [GRS16, PR23]), the generalized harmonic process (e.g., [FG22]), as well as their non-conservative variants in contact with either reversible or non-reversible particle reservoirs (e.g., [Sal23, Sal24] for the analogue results for SEP{\rm SEP}). In particular, intertwining relations, analogous to the ones that we exploit here and which proved to be especially suitable to spectral analyses, are available for all these models. Finally, building on the recent remarkable developments in [HS23, STY23, Sal24], a direction of further investigation consists of deriving sharp (modified) log-Sobolev inequalities and curvature bounds for these particle systems. Our Dirichlet forms’ decompositions may find application also here, although we remark that our intertwining relations do not seem to yield (as they do in our spectral-gap analysis) optimal comparisons. We plan to address all these questions in future works.

1.4. Structure of the paper

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. The upper bound in Theorem 1.1 is proved in Section 2. The proof of the lower bound in Theorem 1.1 occupies the whole Section 3, which is further divided into four subsections. In Section 4, we present the proof of Theorem 1.3. Finally, in the Appendix, we discuss a lookdown representation of SIP{\rm SIP}.

2. Proof of upper bound in Theorem 1.1

In the remainder of the article, since the graph GG is fixed, we may drop the dependence on GG for the objects. For example, we express

gapSIP(G,α)=gapSIP(α)andgapRW(G,α)=gapRW(α).\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm SIP}(G,\alpha)=\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm SIP}(\alpha)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm RW}(G,\alpha)=\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm RW}(\alpha)\ .

We start with establishing the upper bound in Theorem 1.1. The simple idea underlying its proof is that, as in the case of SEP and other systems enjoying a suitable form of consistency/self-duality, observables of a few particles may be “lifted” to observables of many particles, yet yielding coherent statistics. In particular, eigenfunctions for RW⁡(α){\rm RW}(\alpha) “lift” to eigenfunctions for SIPk​(α){\rm SIP}_{k}(\alpha); this is rigorously demonstrated in Lemma 2.2 below.

For each k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, the annihilation operator 𝔞k:ℝΞk−1→ℝΞk\mathfrak{a}_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k-1}}\to\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}} is defined, for g∈ℝΞk−1g\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k-1}} and η∈Ξk\eta\in\Xi_{k}, as

(2.1) 𝔞k​g​(η):=∑x∈Vηx​g​(η−δx),\mathfrak{a}_{k}g(\eta):=\sum_{x\in V}\eta_{x}\,g(\eta-\delta_{x})\ ,

where ℝ∅\mathbb{R}^{\emptyset} is conventionally understood as the space of constants. Intuitively, 𝔞k​g\mathfrak{a}_{k}g evaluates the value at η∈Ξk\eta\in\Xi_{k} by summing up all the values of gg evaluated at a (k−1)(k-1)-particle configuration chosen inside η\eta uniformly at random. This motivates also to say that 𝔞k\mathfrak{a}_{k} corresponds to the operation of “removing a particle uniformly at random”. Moreover, it holds, for every k>ℓ∈ℕk>\ell\in\mathbb{N}, g∈ℝΞℓg\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{\ell}}, and η∈Ξk\eta\in\Xi_{k}, that

(2.2) (𝔞k∘⋯∘𝔞ℓ+1)g(η)=∑ζ∈Ξℓ(∏x∈V(ηxζx))g(ζ).(\mathfrak{a}_{k}\circ\cdots\circ\mathfrak{a}_{\ell+1})g(\eta)=\sum_{\zeta\in\Xi_{\ell}}\left(\prod_{x\in V}{\eta_{x}\choose\zeta_{x}}\right)g(\zeta)\ .

Indeed, the left-hand side of (2.2) can be calculated by summing up the values of gg evaluated at a ℓ\ell-particle configuration chosen from η\eta uniformly, which is exactly the right-hand side of (2.2).

In this section, we use two important properties (both discussed in detail in the Appendix) of 𝔞k\mathfrak{a}_{k}, k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}:

  • •

    the operator 𝔞k:ℝΞk−1→ℝΞk\mathfrak{a}_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k-1}}\to\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}} is injective;

  • •

    it holds that

    (2.3) 𝔞k​Lk−1=Lk​𝔞k.\mathfrak{a}_{k}L_{k-1}=L_{k}\mathfrak{a}_{k}\ .

Especially, (2.3) implies that removing a particle at random first and then running the system (left-hand side) is equivalent, in distribution, to running the system first and then removing a particle at random (right-hand side).

Remark 2.1.

The concept in 𝔞k:ℝΞk−1→ℝΞk\mathfrak{a}_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k-1}}\to\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}} of removing a particle uniformly at random is essential in SIP{\rm SIP}. This is not the case in other related models such as the interchange process or the binomial splitting process. In these examples, the dynamics restricted to a subset of labeled particles is still Markovian and of the same type as the larger system. Thus, therein, one can fix a specific particle and then lift the remaining particle configuration. Such a property holds for SIP{\rm SIP} not for all subsets of particles, but only for subsets chosen uniformly at random. For more details on this property, we refer the interested reader to the Appendix.

The identity (2.3) has the following consequence. Suppose that −Lk−1​g=λ​g-L_{k-1}g=\lambda g holds for some λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R} and non-zero g∈ℝΞk−1g\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k-1}}. Then,

−Lk​(𝔞k​g)=𝔞k​(−Lk−1​g)=𝔞k​(λ​g)=λ​𝔞k​g,-L_{k}(\mathfrak{a}_{k}g)=\mathfrak{a}_{k}(-L_{k-1}g)=\mathfrak{a}_{k}(\lambda g)=\lambda\mathfrak{a}_{k}g\ ,

so that the new function 𝔞k​g∈ℝΞk\mathfrak{a}_{k}g\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}}, which is non-zero since 𝔞k\mathfrak{a}_{k} is injective, is an eigenfunction of −Lk-L_{k} subjected to the same eigenvalue λ\lambda. Thus, the operator 𝔞k\mathfrak{a}_{k} lifts the eigenspace of −Lk−1-L_{k-1} to the eigenspace of −Lk-L_{k}. Then, inductively, the composition 𝔞k∘⋯∘𝔞ℓ+1:ℝΞℓ→ℝΞk\mathfrak{a}_{k}\circ\cdots\circ\mathfrak{a}_{\ell+1}:\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{\ell}}\to\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}} lifts the eigenspace of the operator −Lℓ-L_{\ell} to the eigenspace of −Lk-L_{k} for all ℓ<k∈ℕ\ell<k\in\mathbb{N}. Since all the eigenvalues of −Lℓ-L_{\ell} are also eigenvalues of −Lk-L_{k}, it holds in particular that

gapk(α)≤gapℓ(α).\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{k}(\alpha)\leq\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\ell}(\alpha)\ .

Considering the special case ℓ=1\ell=1 and taking the infimum over all k≥2k\geq 2 in the left-hand side, we have verified the upper bound in Theorem 1.1: for every α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V},

gapSIP(α)≤gapRW(α).\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm SIP}(\alpha)\leq\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm RW}(\alpha)\ .

Before concluding this section, we record a lemma which presents the eigenfunction of −Lk-L_{k} lifted from the original eigenfunction of −Aα-A_{\alpha} subjected to the same eigenvalue.

Lemma 2.2.

Let ψ:V→ℝ\psi:V\to\mathbb{R} be an eigenfunction for −Aα-A_{\alpha} with eigenvalue λ≥0\lambda\geq 0. Then, for every k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, the function fψ,k∈ℝΞkf_{\psi,k}\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}} given by

fψ,k​(η):=∑x∈Vψ⁡(x)​ηx,η∈Ξk,f_{\psi,k}(\eta):=\sum_{x\in V}\psi(x)\,\eta_{x}\ ,\qquad\eta\in\Xi_{k}\ ,

Proof.

Define g∈ℝΞ1g\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{1}} as g⁡(δx):=ψ⁡(x)g(\delta_{x}):=\psi(x). It is clear that gg becomes an eigenfunction for −L1-L_{1} with eigenvalue λ≥0\lambda\geq 0. Substituting ℓ=1\ell=1 in (2.2), we obtain that

(𝔞k∘⋯∘𝔞2)g(η)=∑x∈Vηxg(δx)=∑x∈Vηxψ(x),(\mathfrak{a}_{k}\circ\cdots\circ\mathfrak{a}_{2})g(\eta)=\sum_{x\in V}\eta_{x}\,g(\delta_{x})=\sum_{x\in V}\eta_{x}\,\psi(x)\ ,

so that we have

Since g≠0g\neq 0 (which follows from the fact that ψ\psi is an eigenfunction) and the operators 𝔞2\mathfrak{a}_{2} through 𝔞k\mathfrak{a}_{k} are all injective, fψ,kf_{\psi,k} is a non-zero function.

It remains to verify that −Lk​fψ,k=λ​fψ,k-L_{k}f_{\psi,k}=\lambda f_{\psi,k} holds. This is an easy consequence of (2.4) and the intertwining relation (2.3):

−Lkfψ,k=−Lk(𝔞k∘⋯∘𝔞2)g=(𝔞k∘⋯∘𝔞2)(−L1g)=(𝔞k∘⋯∘𝔞2)(λg)=λfψ,k.-L_{k}f_{\psi,k}=-L_{k}(\mathfrak{a}_{k}\circ\cdots\circ\mathfrak{a}_{2})g=(\mathfrak{a}_{k}\circ\cdots\circ\mathfrak{a}_{2})(-L_{1}g)=(\mathfrak{a}_{k}\circ\cdots\circ\mathfrak{a}_{2})(\lambda g)=\lambda f_{\psi,k}\ .

Thus, we conclude the proof. ∎

3. Proof of lower bound in Theorem 1.1

In this section, we tackle the lower bound in Theorem 1.1; namely, we prove

(3.1) (1∧αmin)​gapRW(α)≤gapSIP(α).(1\wedge\alpha_{\rm min})\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm RW}(\alpha)\leq\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm SIP}(\alpha)\ .

3.1. Preliminaries

In Section 2, we demonstrated that the eigenfunctions of the operator −Lk−1-L_{k-1} are lifted via 𝔞k\mathfrak{a}_{k} to the eigenfunctions of the operator −Lk-L_{k}, thus, ensuring that the eigenvalues of −Lk−1-L_{k-1} are also eigenvalues of −Lk-L_{k}. Hence, to find the remaining eigenvalues of −Lk-L_{k} that do not come from the lifting property of 𝔞k\mathfrak{a}_{k}, since −Lk-L_{k} is self-adjoint, it suffices to investigate functions f∈L2​(μα,k)f\in L^{2}(\mu_{\alpha,k}) (cf. (3.2)) that belong to the orthogonal complement of the image of the operator 𝔞k\mathfrak{a}_{k}. Since 𝔞k\mathfrak{a}_{k} injectively takes all the functions in ℝΞk−1\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k-1}} into ℝΞk\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}}, such an ff should satisfy a certain mean-zero condition subjected to each (k−1)(k-1)-particle configuration:

∑x∈V(ξx+αx)​f​(ξ+δx)=0,ξ∈Ξk−1.\sum_{x\in V}\left(\xi_{x}+\alpha_{x}\right)f(\xi+\delta_{x})=0\ ,\qquad\xi\in\Xi_{k-1}\ .

In this sense, it is natural to define, for k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, the creation operator 𝔞k−1†:ℝΞk→ℝΞk−1\mathfrak{a}_{k-1}^{\dagger}:\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}}\to\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k-1}} as follows: for all f∈ℝΞkf\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}} and ξ∈Ξk−1\xi\in\Xi_{k-1},

𝔞k−1†​f​(ξ):=∑x∈V(ξx+αx)​f​(ξ+δx),\mathfrak{a}_{k-1}^{\dagger}f(\xi):=\sum_{x\in V}\left(\xi_{x}+\alpha_{x}\right)f(\xi+\delta_{x})\ ,

It turns out that the two operators 𝔞k\mathfrak{a}_{k} and 𝔞k−1†\mathfrak{a}_{k-1}^{\dagger} are indeed closely related to each other, as the following proposition shows. For two functions f,g∈ℝΞkf,g\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}}, we define the inner product ⟨f|g⟩α,k\langle f\,|\,g\rangle_{\alpha,k} as

(3.2) ⟨f|g⟩α,k:=∑η∈Ξkμα,k​(η)​f​(η)​g​(η),\left\langle f\,\middle|\,g\right\rangle_{\alpha,k}:=\sum_{\eta\in\Xi_{k}}\mu_{\alpha,k}(\eta)\,f(\eta)\,g(\eta)\ ,

3.2. Decomposition of Dirichlet forms

For k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, we define the Dirichlet form ℰα,k​(f)\mathcal{E}_{\alpha,k}(f) evaluated at f∈ℝΞkf\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}} as

(3.4) ℰα,k​(f):=⟨f|−Lk​f⟩α,k.\mathcal{E}_{\alpha,k}(f):=\langle f\,|\,-L_{k}f\rangle_{\alpha,k}\ .

Moreover, we let 𝒟α​(ϕ)\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}(\phi) denote the Dirichlet form at ϕ∈ℝV\phi\in\mathbb{R}^{V} subjected to RW⁡(α){\rm RW}(\alpha):

(3.5) 𝒟α​(ϕ):=∑x∈Vαx|α|​ϕ​(x)​(−Aα​ϕ)​(x)=1|α|​∑x,y∈Vαx​αy​cx​y​ϕ​(x)​(ϕ⁡(x)−ϕ⁡(y)).\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}(\phi):=\sum_{x\in V}\frac{\alpha_{x}}{|\alpha|}\,\phi(x)\left(-A_{\alpha}\phi\right)(x)=\frac{1}{|\alpha|}\sum_{x,y\in V}\alpha_{x}\alpha_{y}\,c_{xy}\,\phi(x)\left(\phi(x)-\phi(y)\right)\ .

where the second equality holds by part (a) of Proposition 3.1. This implies that the expectation of ff with respect to μα,k\mu_{\alpha,k} is zero, and thus

(3.8) Varα,k​(f)=∑η∈Ξkμα,k​(η)​f​(η)2.{\rm Var}_{\alpha,k}(f)=\sum_{\eta\in\Xi_{k}}\mu_{\alpha,k}(\eta)\,f(\eta)^{2}\ .

In this subsection, we prove the following lemma, which is partially motivated from [HS19]. The idea of proof is to decompose on Ker​𝔞k−1†{\rm Ker}\,\mathfrak{a}_{k-1}^{\dagger} the kk-Dirichlet form ℰα,k​(⋅)\mathcal{E}_{\alpha,k}(\cdot) into lower-order Dirichlet forms 𝒟β​(⋅)\mathcal{D}_{\beta}(\cdot) for some suitably chosen β=β⁡(α)\beta=\beta(\alpha).

Lemma 3.3.

Suppose that f∈Ker​𝔞k−1†f\in{\rm Ker}\,\mathfrak{a}_{k-1}^{\dagger}. Then, we have

3.3. Min-max theorem for eigenvalues

Here, we apply the well-known min-max theorem for eigenvalues (e.g., [SC97, Theorem 1.2.10]) to obtain a lower bound for the term infξ∈Ξk−1gapRW(α+ξ)\inf_{\xi\in\Xi_{k-1}}\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm RW}(\alpha+\xi) that appears in Lemma 3.3.

For every α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V} and k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, it holds that

Let us compare the Dirichlet forms and the L2L^{2}-norms associated to RW⁡(α){\rm RW}(\alpha) and RW⁡(α+ξ){\rm RW}(\alpha+\xi). We claim that, for all ϕ:V→ℝ\phi:V\to\mathbb{R} and ξ∈Ξk−1\xi\in\Xi_{k-1},

(3.12) |α||α|+k−1​𝒟α​(ϕ)≤𝒟α+ξ​(ϕ),αmin​(|α|+k−1)|α|​(αmin+k−1)​‖ϕ‖L2​(α+ξ)2≤‖ϕ‖L2​(α)2​.\frac{|\alpha|}{|\alpha|+k-1}\,\mathcal{D}_{\alpha}(\phi)\leq\mathcal{D}_{\alpha+\xi}(\phi)\ ,\qquad\frac{\alpha_{\rm min}(|\alpha|+k-1)}{|\alpha|(\alpha_{\rm min}+k-1)}\,\left\|\phi\right\|_{L^{2}(\alpha+\xi)}^{2}\leq\left\|\phi\right\|_{L^{2}(\alpha)}^{2}\;\text{.}

≤12​∑x,y∈Vcx​y​αx+ξx|α|+k−1​(αy+ξy)​(ϕ⁡(x)−ϕ⁡(y))2=𝒟α+ξ​(ϕ).\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x,y\in V}c_{xy}\,\frac{\alpha_{x}+\xi_{x}}{|\alpha|+k-1}\left(\alpha_{y}+\xi_{y}\right)\left(\phi(x)-\phi(y)\right)^{2}=\mathcal{D}_{\alpha+\xi}(\phi)\ .

≤∑x∈Vαx|α|​ϕ​(x)2,\displaystyle\leq\sum_{x\in V}\frac{\alpha_{x}}{|\alpha|}\,\phi(x)^{2}\ ,

where for the first and second inequalities we used, respectively,

αminαmin+k−1≤αxαx+k−1andξx≤k−1,x∈V.\frac{\alpha_{\rm min}}{\alpha_{\rm min}+k-1}\leq\frac{\alpha_{x}}{\alpha_{x}+k-1}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\xi_{x}\leq k-1\ ,\qquad x\in V\ .

By applying as, e.g., in [SC97, Theorem 1.2.11] the min-max theorem for eigenvalues and the comparison inequalities in (3.12), we get

3.4. Proof of lower bound in Theorem 1.1

Finally, we present a formal proof of the lower bound in Theorem 1.1.

Proof of lower bound in Theorem 1.1.

(3.13) (1∧αmin)​gapRW(α)≤gapk(α),k∈ℕ.(1\wedge\alpha_{\rm min})\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm RW}(\alpha)\leq\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{k}(\alpha)\ ,\qquad k\in\mathbb{N}\ .

We proceed by an induction on k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. First, (3.13) is obvious for k=1k=1. Next, suppose that (3.13) holds for k−1k-1, and we prove (3.13) for k≥2k\geq 2. By (3.6) and Lemma 3.2, we have

Since 𝔞k:ℝΞk−1→ℝΞk\mathfrak{a}_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k-1}}\to\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}} lifts all the eigenfunctions of −Lk−1-L_{k-1} to −Lk-L_{k}, it is readily verified that

where the inequality holds by the induction hypothesis. Moreover, by Lemmas 3.3 and 3.4, we have

It is straightforward to check that

Collecting (3.14), (3.15), (3.16), and (3.17), we conclude that

gapk(α)≥(1∧αmin)​gapRW(α),\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{k}(\alpha)\geq(1\wedge\alpha_{\rm min})\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm RW}(\alpha)\ ,

4. Proof of Theorem 1.3

the BEP and SIP are related via an intertwining relation (e.g., [RS18, Proposition 5.1]): for all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} and f∈ℝΞkf\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}}, we have

(4.1) ℒ​Λ​f=Λ​Lk​f,with​Λ:ℝΞk→ℝΔV,Λ​f​(ζ):=∑η∈Ξk(∏x∈Vζxηxηx!)​f​(η).\mathcal{L}\varLambda f=\varLambda L_{k}f\ ,\qquad\text{with}\ \varLambda:\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}}\to\mathbb{R}^{\Delta_{V}}\ ,\ \varLambda f(\zeta):=\sum_{\eta\in\Xi_{k}}\left(\prod_{x\in V}\frac{\zeta_{x}^{\eta_{x}}}{\eta_{x}!}\right)f(\eta)\ .

Thanks to this connection and the assertion in Theorem 1.1, once we check that the spectrum of ℒ\mathcal{L} on L2​(ΔV,π)L^{2}(\Delta_{V},\pi) is pure point, the proof of Theorem 1.3 boils down to verifying the validity of the following two claims:

  • •

    −gapRW(α)-\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm RW}(\alpha) belongs to the spectrum of ℒ\mathcal{L} (Lemma 4.1);

  • •

    each eigenvalue of ℒ\mathcal{L} is also an eigenvalue of LkL_{k} given in (1.1), for some k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} (Lemma 4.2).

The fact that ℒ\mathcal{L} has a pure point spectrum may be shown as follows. The generator ℒ\mathcal{L} is self-adjoint on L2​(ΔV,π)L^{2}(\Delta_{V},\pi), thus, its spectrum is real. Moreover, for every k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, the generator ℒ\mathcal{L} (see (1.4)) is easily seen to leave invariant the subspace of all polynomials of degree at most kk in the variables (ζx)x∈V(\zeta_{x})_{x\in V}. Each of these subspaces is finite-dimensional, ensuring a decomposition of ℒ\mathcal{L} in terms of finitely-many eigenvalue/eigenfunction pairs when restricted therein. By density of polynomials in L2​(ΔV,π)L^{2}(\Delta_{V},\pi), this eigendecomposition, suitably orthonormalized, gives rise to an orthonormal basis of L2​(ΔV,π)L^{2}(\Delta_{V},\pi) consisting of eigenfunctions of ℒ\mathcal{L}. In conclusion, the generator ℒ\mathcal{L} on L2​(ΔV,π)L^{2}(\Delta_{V},\pi) admits a pure point real spectrum.

We verify that −gapRW(α)-\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm RW}(\alpha) belongs to the spectrum of ℒ\mathcal{L} in the following lemma, whose proof is analogous to that of Lemma 2.2.

Lemma 4.1.

Let ψ:V→ℝ\psi:V\to\mathbb{R} be an eigenfunction for AαA_{\alpha} associated to −gapRW(α)-\mathop{\rm gap}\nolimits_{\rm RW}(\alpha). Then, the first-order polynomial f:ΔV→ℝf:\Delta_{V}\to\mathbb{R} in the variables (ζx)x∈V(\zeta_{x})_{x\in V} given by

(4.2) fψ​(ζ):=∑x∈Vψ⁡(x)​ζx,ζ∈ΔV,f_{\psi}(\zeta):=\sum_{x\in V}\psi(x)\,\zeta_{x}\ ,\qquad\zeta\in\Delta_{V}\ ,

is an eigenfunction for ℒ\mathcal{L} associated to the same eigenvalue.

Proof.

Let g∈ℝΞ1g\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{1}} be given by g⁡(δx):=ψ⁡(x)g(\delta_{x}):=\psi(x), x∈Vx\in V. Then, recalling (4.1), the function in (4.2) reads as

fψ=Λ​g.f_{\psi}=\varLambda\,g\ .

In view of this representation for fψf_{\psi}, the injectivity of Λ\varLambda, and the intertwining relation (4.1), the desired claim follows as in the proof of Lemma 2.2. ∎

In the following lemma, we show that each eigenfunction ff of ℒ\mathcal{L} corresponds to an eigenfunction of LkL_{k}, for some k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, both associated to the same eigenvalue.

Lemma 4.2.

Let f∈L2​(ΔV,π)f\in L^{2}(\Delta_{V},\pi) be a non-constant eigenfunction of ℒ\mathcal{L} associated to the eigenvalue −λ<0-\lambda<0. Then, there exist k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} and g∈ℝΞkg\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}} such that gg is an eigenfunction of LkL_{k} associated to the eigenvalue −λ<0-\lambda<0.

Proof.

By the discussion at the beginning of this section, all eigenfunctions of ℒ\mathcal{L} are polynomials in the variables (ζx)x∈V(\zeta_{x})_{x\in V} of degree at most kk, for some k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. Hence, we may rewrite ff as follows:

(4.3) f⁡(ζ)=∑ℓ=0k∑η∈Ξℓgℓ​(η)​∏x∈Vζxηxηx!=∑ℓ=0kΛ​gℓ​(ζ),f(\zeta)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{k}\sum_{\eta\in\Xi_{\ell}}g_{\ell}(\eta)\,\prod_{x\in V}\frac{\zeta_{x}^{\eta_{x}}}{\eta_{x}!}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{k}\varLambda g_{\ell}(\zeta)\ ,

for some k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} and functions gℓ∈ℝΞℓg_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{\ell}}, ℓ=0,1,…,k\ell=0,1,\ldots,k. In the formula above, we included the factor (∏x∈Vηx!)−1\left(\prod_{x\in V}\eta_{x}!\right)^{-1} just for convenience, so to recover an expression like that in (4.1). Now, by applying the generator ℒ\mathcal{L} to the function ff in (4.3) and using (4.1), we get

ℒ​f​(ζ)=∑ℓ=0k∑η∈ΞℓLℓ​gℓ​(η)​∏x∈Vζxηxηx!=∑ℓ=0kΛ​Lℓ​gℓ​(ζ).\mathcal{L}f(\zeta)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{k}\sum_{\eta\in\Xi_{\ell}}L_{\ell}g_{\ell}(\eta)\,\prod_{x\in V}\frac{\zeta_{x}^{\eta_{x}}}{\eta_{x}!}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{k}\varLambda L_{\ell}g_{\ell}(\zeta)\ .

The assumption ℒ​f+λ​f=0\mathcal{L}f+\lambda f=0 yields

∑ℓ=0k∑η∈Ξℓ{Lℓ​gℓ​(η)+λ​gℓ​(η)}​∏x∈Vζxηxηx!=0,\sum_{\ell=0}^{k}\sum_{\eta\in\Xi_{\ell}}\left\{L_{\ell}g_{\ell}(\eta)+\lambda g_{\ell}(\eta)\right\}\prod_{x\in V}\frac{\zeta_{x}^{\eta_{x}}}{\eta_{x}!}=0\ ,

which holds for all ζ∈ΔV\zeta\in\Delta_{V} if and only if each term in the bracket equals zero. Finally, since at least one among the functions gℓg_{\ell}, ℓ>0\ell>0, is non-zero, this ensures that −λ<0-\lambda<0 is an eigenvalue for LℓL_{\ell}. ∎

Appendix A Lookdown representation for SIP{\rm SIP}

In this appendix, we provide a self-contained proof of the injectivity of the operator 𝔞k:ℝΞk−1→ℝΞk\mathfrak{a}_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k-1}}\to\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}} (2.1) and the intertwining relation (2.3). Relations of this kind play a major role in the context of interacting particle systems and population genetics (e.g., [Lig05, GKRV09, EK19, CGR21, EKLRT24] and references therein). For the particular case of SIP{\rm SIP}, we know at least three proofs of the identity in (2.3). The first one is by a direct (but lengthy) computation; the second one is by Lie algebraic representations of the generator LkL_{k} (see (1.1)) in terms of products of “single-site” analogues of 𝔞k\mathfrak{a}_{k} and 𝔞k−1†\mathfrak{a}_{k-1}^{\dagger} (e.g., [GKRV09]); the third one is by a lookdown representation of SIP{\rm SIP}, in the spirit of the seminal work [DK96]. For this appendix, we follow this third approach, as it seems the least known, yet, it provides a probabilistic insight into the identity in (2.1) and several related properties of the particle system.

In a nutshell, the main idea is to describe SIP{\rm SIP} as arising from a non-symmetric hierarchical version of it, for which the corresponding intertwining relation is then straightforward. A hierarchical structure is recovered by first assigning labels to particles (which do not change all throughout the dynamics), and then devising jumping rates which depend also on labels. Following a standard terminology, we imagine labeled particles being assigned lanes, stacked one on top of the other, so that the particle with the smallest label represents the bottom particle, whereas the highest-label particle is the top particle. In this language, we derive SIP{\rm SIP} from a model in which high particles “look down” to low particles, but not vice versa.

Let us now introduce some general notation to describe the position and evolution of these labeled particles, and fix an integer k≥2k\geq 2, representing the total number of labeled particles, all throughout this appendix. For all 𝐱=(x1,…,xk)∈Vk\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\in V^{k} and permutations σ∈Sk\sigma\in S_{k}, let σ​𝐱:=(xσ⁡(1),…,xσ⁡(k))∈Vk\sigma\mathbf{x}:=(x_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,x_{\sigma(k)})\in V^{k}. Further, let 𝒮k:ℝVk→ℝVk\mathcal{S}_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{V^{k}}\to\mathbb{R}^{V^{k}} denote the symmetrization operator: for all φ∈ℝVk\varphi\in\mathbb{R}^{V^{k}} and 𝐱∈Vk\mathbf{x}\in V^{k},

(A.1) 𝒮k​φ​(𝐱):=1k!​∑σ∈Skφ⁡(σ​𝐱).\mathcal{S}_{k}\varphi(\mathbf{x}):=\frac{1}{k!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{k}}\varphi(\sigma\mathbf{x})\ .

Finally, the function Φk:Vk→Ξk\Phi_{k}:V^{k}\to\Xi_{k}, defined as

(A.2) Φk​(𝐱):=∑i=1kδxi,\Phi_{k}(\mathbf{x}):=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\delta_{x_{i}}\ ,

removes the labels from particles.

A.1. Annihilation operators

Next to the annihilation operator 𝔞k:ℝΞk−1→ℝΞk\mathfrak{a}_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k-1}}\to\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}} defined in (2.1) and well-suited for unlabeled particle configurations, we introduce a top-particle annihilation operator 𝒥k:ℝVk−1→ℝVk\mathcal{J}_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{V^{k-1}}\to\mathbb{R}^{V^{k}}, given, for all φ∈ℝVk−1\varphi\in\mathbb{R}^{V^{k-1}}, by

(A.3) 𝒥k​φ​(𝐱):=φ⁡(x1,…,xk−1),𝐱=(x1,…,xk)∈Vk.\mathcal{J}_{k}\varphi(\mathbf{x}):=\varphi(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k-1})\ ,\qquad\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\in V^{k}\ .

Up to permuting the labels uniformly at random, 𝔞k\mathfrak{a}_{k} is just the unlabeled version of this operator (up to a constant factor). This is the content of the following lemma.

Lemma A.1.

For all g∈ℝΞk−1g\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k-1}}, we have 𝔞k​g∘Φk=k​𝒮k​𝒥k​(g∘Φk−1)\mathfrak{a}_{k}g\circ\Phi_{k}=k\,\mathcal{S}_{k}\mathcal{J}_{k}(g\circ\Phi_{k-1}).

Proof.

For every 𝐱=(x1,…,xk)∈Vk\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\in V^{k} and φ:=g∘Φk−1∈ℝVk−1\varphi:=g\circ\Phi_{k-1}\in\mathbb{R}^{V^{k-1}}, we get

1k​𝔞k​g​(Φk​(𝐱))\displaystyle\frac{1}{k}\,\mathfrak{a}_{k}g(\Phi_{k}(\mathbf{x})) =1k​∑i=1kg⁡(Φk​(𝐱)−δxi)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}g(\Phi_{k}(\mathbf{x})-\delta_{x_{i}})
=1k∑i=1k1(k−1)!∑σ∈Sk:σ⁡(k)=iφ(xσ⁡(1),…,xσ⁡(k−1))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{1}{(k-1)!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{k}\,:\,\sigma(k)=i}\varphi(x_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,x_{\sigma(k-1)})
=1k!​∑σ∈Sk𝒥k​φ​(σ​𝐱)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{k!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{k}}\mathcal{J}_{k}\varphi(\sigma\mathbf{x})
=𝒮k​𝒥k​φ​(𝐱),\displaystyle=\mathcal{S}_{k}\mathcal{J}_{k}\varphi(\mathbf{x})\ ,

where we used the definition of 𝔞k\mathfrak{a}_{k} in (2.1), that of φ\varphi and 𝒮k−1\mathcal{S}_{k-1}, and finally that of 𝒥k\mathcal{J}_{k} and 𝒮k\mathcal{S}_{k}. This concludes the proof of the lemma. ∎

The next lemma establishes the injectivity of both annihilation operators, a property that we used, e.g., for the proof of the upper bound in Theorem 1.1.

Lemma A.2 (Injectivity).

Both 𝒥k:ℝVk−1→ℝVk\mathcal{J}_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{V^{k-1}}\to\mathbb{R}^{V^{k}} and 𝔞k:ℝΞk−1→ℝΞk\mathfrak{a}_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k-1}}\to\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}} are injective.

Proof.

The injectivity of 𝒥k\mathcal{J}_{k} is obvious from the definition in (A.3), because 𝒥k​φ​(𝐱)=0∈ℝVk\mathcal{J}_{k}\varphi(\mathbf{x})=0\in\mathbb{R}^{V^{k}} if and only if φ⁡(x1,…,xk−1)=0∈ℝVk−1\varphi(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k-1})=0\in\mathbb{R}^{V^{k-1}}, for all 𝐱=(x1,…,xk)∈Vk\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\in V^{k}. The proof of injectivity of 𝔞k\mathfrak{a}_{k} does not follow at once from the representation in Lemma A.1, because 𝒮k\mathcal{S}_{k} is not one-to-one (recall that k≥2k\geq 2); therefore, we take an alternative route.

Partition Ξk−1\Xi_{k-1} into disjoint subsets {Ξk−1(ℓ)}ℓ=0,1,…,k−1\{\Xi_{k-1}^{(\ell)}\}_{\ell=0,1,\ldots,k-1}, given by

Ξk−1(0):=∅,Ξk−1(ℓ):={ξ∈Ξk−1:maxx∈Vξx=k−ℓ},ℓ=1,…,k−1.\Xi_{k-1}^{(0)}:=\varnothing\ ,\qquad\Xi_{k-1}^{(\ell)}:=\left\{\xi\in\Xi_{k-1}:\max_{x\in V}\xi_{x}=k-\ell\right\}\ ,\quad\ell=1,\ldots,k-1\ .

Observe that Ξk−1(ℓ)\Xi_{k-1}^{(\ell)} may be empty. The injectivity of 𝔞k\mathfrak{a}_{k} follows from the following claim: for all g∈ℝΞk−1g\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k-1}} and ℓ=1,…,k−1\ell=1,\ldots,k-1,

(A.4) 𝔞k​g=0andg=0​on​Ξk−1(ℓ−1)implyg=0​on​Ξk−1(ℓ),\mathfrak{a}_{k}g=0\quad\text{and}\quad g=0\ \text{on}\ \Xi_{k-1}^{(\ell-1)}\quad\text{imply}\quad g=0\ \text{on}\ \Xi_{k-1}^{(\ell)}\ ,

where we interpret “g=0g=0 on ∅\varnothing” as a void condition. We now prove (A.4) for ℓ=1,…,k−1\ell=1,\ldots,k-1. Consider ξ∈Ξk−1(ℓ)\xi\in\Xi_{k-1}^{(\ell)} with ξy=maxx∈V⁡ξx\xi_{y}=\max_{x\in V}\xi_{x}; then,

0=𝔞k​g​(ξ+δy)=∑x∈V(ξx+δx,y)​g​(ξ−δx+δy)=(ξy+1)​g​(ξ),0=\mathfrak{a}_{k}g(\xi+\delta_{y})=\sum_{x\in V}(\xi_{x}+\delta_{x,y})\,g(\xi-\delta_{x}+\delta_{y})=(\xi_{y}+1)\,g(\xi)\ ,

where the first identity used the assumption 𝔞k​g=0\mathfrak{a}_{k}g=0 on Ξk\Xi_{k}, the second one simply used the definition of 𝔞k​g​(ξ+δy)\mathfrak{a}_{k}g(\xi+\delta_{y}), whereas the last one used that ξ−δx+δy∈Ξk−1(ℓ−1)\xi-\delta_{x}+\delta_{y}\in\Xi_{k-1}^{(\ell-1)} for all x≠yx\neq y and the assumption that g=0g=0 on Ξk−1(ℓ−1)\Xi_{k-1}^{(\ell-1)}. This yields (A.4) and, thus, the desired result. ∎

A.2. Labeled versions of SIP{\rm SIP} and intertwining relations

There are at least two labeled versions of SIPk​(G,α){\rm SIP}_{k}(G,\alpha), depending on how one models the interaction of the labeled particles (the non-interacting part of the dynamics, namely, the rate cx​y​αyc_{xy}\,\alpha_{y} to jump from xx to y∈Vy\in V, is the same for the two models): the symmetric and the lookdown versions (see also Remark A.6 below). These models may be informally described as follows.

Let two labeled particles be sitting on xx and y∈Vy\in V, respectively. In the symmetric version, they interact with rate 2​cx​y≥02c_{xy}\geq 0 and, regardless of their labels, either one of them joins, with probability 1/21/2, the site of the other one. This is described by the following generator, which acts on functions φ∈ℝVk\varphi\in\mathbb{R}^{V^{k}} and 𝐱∈Vk\mathbf{x}\in V^{k}, as

(A.5) ℒk​φ​(𝐱)=∑x,y∈Vcx​y​∑i=1kδx,xi​(αy+∑j=1kδy,xj)​(φ⁡(𝐱iy)−φ⁡(𝐱)),\mathcal{L}_{k}\varphi(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{x,y\in V}c_{xy}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\delta_{x,x_{i}}\bigg(\alpha_{y}+\sum_{j=1}^{k}\delta_{y,x_{j}}\bigg)(\varphi(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{y})-\varphi(\mathbf{x}))\ ,

where 𝐱iy∈Vk\mathbf{x}_{i}^{y}\in V^{k} denotes the configuration in which the it​hi^{th} coordinate of 𝐱∈Vk\mathbf{x}\in V^{k} is set equal to y∈Vy\in V. In the lookdown version, two labeled particles at x,y∈Vx,y\in V still interact at rate 2​cx​y2c_{xy}, but, with probability one, only the particle with the higher label jumps on top of the low-label one. This dynamics is encoded in the following generator:

(A.6) ^​ℒk​φ​(𝐱)=∑x,y∈Vcx​y​∑i=1kδx,xi​(αy+2​∑j=1i−1δy,xj)​(φ⁡(𝐱iy)−φ⁡(𝐱)).\widehat{}\mathcal{L}_{k}\varphi(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{x,y\in V}c_{xy}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\delta_{x,x_{i}}\bigg(\alpha_{y}+2\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\delta_{y,x_{j}}\bigg)(\varphi(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{y})-\varphi(\mathbf{x}))\ .

Consequently, in this second model, the first/bottom particle moves as RW⁡(G,α){\rm RW}(G,\alpha), independently from all the other particles. More generally, the it​hi^{th} particle is influenced by each particle with label j<ij<i, and not by those with label j>ij>i. In particular, removing the top particle from the lookdown process either at time t=0t=0 or time t>0t>0 does not affect in any way the evolution of the first k−1k-1 particles. At the level of finite-dimensional distributions, this simple consideration implies the following intertwining relation for the lookdown system, as explained in the following lemma.

Lemma A.3 (Intertwining for lookdown process).

We have 𝒥k​^​ℒk−1=^​ℒk​𝒥k\mathcal{J}_{k}\widehat{}\mathcal{L}_{k-1}=\widehat{}\mathcal{L}_{k}\mathcal{J}_{k}.

Proof.

The claim follows at once from the definition (A.3) of 𝒥k\mathcal{J}_{k} and the fact that the action of ^​ℒk\widehat{}\mathcal{L}_{k} (see (A.6)) on functions in ℝVk\mathbb{R}^{V^{k}} that are constant with respect to the kt​hk^{th} coordinate gives back the action of ^​ℒk−1\widehat{}\mathcal{L}_{k-1}. ∎

Clearly, removing labels from the symmetric model (see (A.5)) yields back SIPk​(G,α){\rm SIP}_{k}(G,\alpha), whose generator LkL_{k} is given in (1.1). At the level of finite-dimensional distributions, this means that

(A.7) 𝒮k​ℒk​(f∘Φk)=ℒk​𝒮k​(f∘Φk)=(Lk​f)∘Φk,f∈ℝΞk.\mathcal{S}_{k}\mathcal{L}_{k}(f\circ\Phi_{k})=\mathcal{L}_{k}\mathcal{S}_{k}(f\circ\Phi_{k})=(L_{k}f)\circ\Phi_{k}\ ,\qquad f\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}}\ .

We remark that this fact holds true for any particles’ labeling, since the dynamics does not actually depend on labels. What is slightly less evident is that, at any time, we obtain the distribution of SIPk​(G,α){\rm SIP}_{k}(G,\alpha) after removing the labels of the lookdown model, provided that the particles are initially labeled uniformly at random. This identity in law is one of the remarkable achievements of [DK96], which has been considerably generalized since then (e.g., [EK19, EKLRT24] and references therein). We provide a proof for our case below. For this purpose, recall the definitions (A.1), (A.6), (A.2) and (1.1).

Proposition A.4 (From lookdown to SIP{\rm SIP}).

For all f∈ℝΞkf\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k}}, we have

𝒮k​^​ℒk​(f∘Φk)=(Lk​f)∘Φk.\mathcal{S}_{k}\widehat{}\mathcal{L}_{k}(f\circ\Phi_{k})=(L_{k}f)\circ\Phi_{k}\ .
Proof.

In view of (A.7), it suffices to prove

(A.8) 𝒮k​^​ℒk=ℒk​𝒮k\mathcal{S}_{k}\widehat{}\mathcal{L}_{k}=\mathcal{L}_{k}\mathcal{S}_{k}

Moreover, we find more instructive to show the details only for the case k=2k=2 (which was also discussed in [FGS22, Section 4.2.3]). In fact, the general case k≥2k\geq 2 follows (up to some notational complications) from this case k=2k=2, because, by linearity, one can deal separately with terms involving different pairs of particles at the time. Henceforth, let us prove (A.8) for k=2k=2. Fix the positions of the two particles, say x,y∈Vx,y\in V. Then, for all φ∈ℝV2\varphi\in\mathbb{R}^{V^{2}}, we have

𝒮2​^​ℒ2​φ​(x,y)\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{2}\widehat{}\mathcal{L}_{2}\varphi(x,y) =12​(^​ℒ2​φ​(x,y)+^​ℒ2​φ​(y,x))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\big(\widehat{}\mathcal{L}_{2}\varphi(x,y)+\widehat{}\mathcal{L}_{2}\varphi(y,x)\big)
=cx​y​αy2​(2​φ​(y,y)−φ⁡(y,x)−φ⁡(x,y))\displaystyle=\frac{c_{xy}\,\alpha_{y}}{2}\big(2\varphi(y,y)-\varphi(y,x)-\varphi(x,y)\big)
+cx​y​αx2​(2​φ​(x,x)−φ⁡(y,x)−φ⁡(x,y))\displaystyle+\frac{c_{xy}\,\alpha_{x}}{2}\big(2\varphi(x,x)-\varphi(y,x)-\varphi(x,y)\big)
+cx​y2​(2​φ​(y,y)−2​φ​(x,y)+2​φ​(x,x)−2​φ​(y,x))\displaystyle+\frac{c_{xy}}{2}\big(2\varphi(y,y)-2\varphi(x,y)+2\varphi(x,x)-2\varphi(y,x)\big)
=cx​y​αy​(𝒮2​φ​(y,y)−𝒮2​φ​(x,y))\displaystyle=c_{xy}\,\alpha_{y}\big(\mathcal{S}_{2}\varphi(y,y)-\mathcal{S}_{2}\varphi(x,y)\big)
+cx​y​αy​(𝒮2​φ​(x,x)−𝒮2​φ​(x,y))\displaystyle+c_{xy}\,\alpha_{y}\big(\mathcal{S}_{2}\varphi(x,x)-\mathcal{S}_{2}\varphi(x,y)\big)
+cx​y​(𝒮2​φ​(y,y)+𝒮2​φ​(x,x)−2​𝒮2​φ​(x,y))=ℒ2​𝒮2​φ​(x,y).\displaystyle+c_{xy}\big(\mathcal{S}_{2}\varphi(y,y)+\mathcal{S}_{2}\varphi(x,x)-2\mathcal{S}_{2}\varphi(x,y)\big)=\mathcal{L}_{2}\mathcal{S}_{2}\varphi(x,y)\ .

This concludes the proof. ∎

We now have all we need to prove the intertwining relation (2.3).

Proposition A.5 (Intertwining for SIP{\rm SIP}).

We have 𝔞k​Lk−1=Lk​𝔞k\mathfrak{a}_{k}L_{k-1}=L_{k}\mathfrak{a}_{k}.

Proof.

Clearly, we have

(A.9) 𝒮k​𝒥k=𝒮k​𝒥k​𝒮k−1.\mathcal{S}_{k}\mathcal{J}_{k}=\mathcal{S}_{k}\mathcal{J}_{k}\mathcal{S}_{k-1}\ .

Hence, for all f∈ℝΞk−1f\in\mathbb{R}^{\Xi_{k-1}}, we get

1k​(𝔞k​Lk−1​f)∘Φk\displaystyle\frac{1}{k}\,(\mathfrak{a}_{k}L_{k-1}f)\circ\Phi_{k} =𝒮k​𝒥k​((Lk−1​f)∘Φk−1)\displaystyle=\mathcal{S}_{k}\mathcal{J}_{k}((L_{k-1}f)\circ\Phi_{k-1}) ⟸Lemma A.1\displaystyle\Longleftarrow\ \text{Lemma \ref{lem:ann-representation}}
=𝒮k​𝒥k​ℒk−1​𝒮k−1​(f∘Φk−1)\displaystyle=\mathcal{S}_{k}\mathcal{J}_{k}\mathcal{L}_{k-1}\mathcal{S}_{k-1}(f\circ\Phi_{k-1}) ⟸Eq. (A.7)\displaystyle\Longleftarrow\ \text{Eq.\ \eqref{eq:gen-gen-sym}}
=𝒮k​𝒥k​𝒮k−1​^​ℒk−1​(f∘Φk−1)\displaystyle=\mathcal{S}_{k}\mathcal{J}_{k}\mathcal{S}_{k-1}\widehat{}\mathcal{L}_{k-1}(f\circ\Phi_{k-1}) ⟸Proposition A.4\displaystyle\Longleftarrow\ \text{Proposition \ref{prop:lookdown-sip}}
=𝒮k​𝒥k​^​ℒk−1​(f∘Φk−1)\displaystyle=\mathcal{S}_{k}\mathcal{J}_{k}\widehat{}\mathcal{L}_{k-1}(f\circ\Phi_{k-1}) ⟸Eq. (A.9)\displaystyle\Longleftarrow\ \text{Eq.\ \eqref{eq:S-J-S}}
=𝒮k​^​ℒk​𝒥k​(f∘Φk−1)\displaystyle=\mathcal{S}_{k}\widehat{}\mathcal{L}_{k}\mathcal{J}_{k}(f\circ\Phi_{k-1}) ⟸Lemma A.3\displaystyle\Longleftarrow\ \text{Lemma \ref{lemma:intertwining-lookdown}}
=ℒk​𝒮k​𝒥k​(f∘Φk−1)\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}_{k}\mathcal{S}_{k}\mathcal{J}_{k}(f\circ\Phi_{k-1}) ⟸Proposition A.4\displaystyle\Longleftarrow\ \text{Proposition \ref{prop:lookdown-sip}}
=1k​ℒk​𝒮k​((𝔞k​f)∘Φk)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{k}\mathcal{L}_{k}\mathcal{S}_{k}((\mathfrak{a}_{k}f)\circ\Phi_{k}) ⟸Lemma A.1\displaystyle\Longleftarrow\ \text{Lemma \ref{lem:ann-representation}}
=1k​(Lk​𝔞k​f)∘Φk,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{k}(L_{k}\mathfrak{a}_{k}f)\circ\Phi_{k}\ , ⟸Eq. (A.7)\displaystyle\Longleftarrow\ \text{Eq.\ \eqref{eq:gen-gen-sym}}

where for the second-to-last line we also used that 𝒮k2=𝒮k\mathcal{S}_{k}^{2}=\mathcal{S}_{k}. ∎

We conclude this appendix with a few comments on stationarity and time-reversal of the lookdown process. We leave the verification of these claims to the reader.

Remark A.6 (Invariant measure & time-reversal).

For both symmetric and lookdown models,

ωk​(𝐱):=αx1(αx2+δx2,x1)⋯(αxk+∑j=1k−1δxk,xj)|α|(|α|+1)⋯(|α|+k−1),𝐱=(x1,…,xk)∈Vk,\omega_{k}(\mathbf{x}):=\frac{\alpha_{x_{1}}\big(\alpha_{x_{2}}+\delta_{x_{2},x_{1}}\big)\cdots\big(\alpha_{x_{k}}+\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\delta_{x_{k},x_{j}}\big)}{|\alpha|\big(|\alpha|+1\big)\cdots\big(|\alpha|+k-1\big)}\ ,\qquad\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\in V^{k}\ ,

is the unique invariant measure (provided GG is connected). More specifically, the symmetric model is reversible with respect to ωk\omega_{k}, while this is not the case for the lookdown one. This, in particular, implies that the lookdown model admits a non-trivial time reversal process. The exact form of the corresponding infinitesimal generator ^​ℒk∗\widehat{}\mathcal{L}_{k}^{*} does not play a role in our argument; we only mention that the jump rate of the it​hi^{th} particle may depend on the positions of all the other particles. Finally, SIPk​(G,α){\rm SIP}_{k}(G,\alpha) arises also from this time-reversal process: 𝒮k​^​ℒk=^​ℒk∗​𝒮k\mathcal{S}_{k}\widehat{}\mathcal{L}_{k}=\widehat{}\mathcal{L}_{k}^{*}\mathcal{S}_{k}, and ^​ℒk∗\widehat{}\mathcal{L}_{k}^{*} satisfies an intertwining relation with the “labeled” version of 𝔞k−1†\mathfrak{a}_{k-1}^{\dagger}.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research.
